Moonshot hasn't responded publicly, and according to TechCrunch and Seeking Alpha, the full Kimi K3 model weights are still set to be released publicly by July 27th — so we'll likely learn more as researchers get a chance to examine it directly.

JENNY: Meanwhile, on the other side of the AI race, Google's Gemini 3.5 Pro still hasn't had its broader public launch. It's been pushed back several months now after internal testing reportedly showed it falling short on coding and complex reasoning tasks. It remains limited to an enterprise preview on Vertex AI, with no new launch date given.

ANDREW: So between the two stories, you've got Washington accusing Beijing of stealing a frontier model, and Google quietly admitting its own frontier model isn't ready. Not exactly a confidence-inspiring week for anyone trying to bet on which lab actually has the best technology.

JENNY: That's the tension right now — the public rhetoric is all about speed and dominance, but underneath it, both the accusation and the delay are really about how hard it still is to reliably build and defend a frontier-level model.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's happening on the mortgage side today? I know Freddie Mac's weekly numbers usually land Thursday mornings.

JENNY: They do, and today's print is a big one to watch. Freddie Mac's last confirmed reading, from July 16th, had the 30-year fixed averaging 6.55 percent, up from 6.49 percent the week before. The Mortgage Bankers Association's own survey, for the week ending July 17th, showed the 30-year conforming rate even higher, at 6.69 percent — the highest level since last August.

ANDREW: So which number do borrowers actually trust more right now?

JENNY: They measure slightly different things, but they're both pointing the same direction — up. The MBA also reported overall mortgage applications rose 1.9 percent that week, with purchase activity jumping 6 percent even as refinancing pulled back 2 percent, which tells you buyers are still trying to lock in before rates climb further. Interestingly, today's ten-year Treasury yield actually ticked down slightly despite the oil spike, so it's not guaranteed this week's Freddie Mac number jumps sharply — but if oil stays near 98 dollars for more than a few days, that pressure usually finds its way into mortgage pricing.

ANDREW: Worth flagging too — the median existing home price hit a record 440,600 dollars in June, according to HousingWire, so buyers are contending with both higher rates and higher prices at the same time.

JENNY: That's a tough combination for a first-time buyer especially. Any relief in sight, or is this just the new normal for now?

ANDREW: Not in the immediate term. Until the Fed's path gets clearer after next week's meeting, and until we see whether this oil shock passes or sticks around, lenders are likely to keep pricing in extra caution. The one thing working in buyers' favor is that purchase applications are still rising even at these rates, which tells you demand hasn't collapsed — people are adjusting their budgets rather than waiting on the sidelines.

JENNY: Speaking of Jacksonville, let's head there now. Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a hot one today — sunny with afternoon thunderstorms likely, a high near 96 degrees, and the heat index climbing as high as 108.

JENNY: The city's Planning Commission holds its first public hearing today on the Franklin Arms rezoning, at 1 p.m. at the Edward Ball Building downtown. This is the senior housing redevelopment we've been following — a 50 million dollar project that would replace the deteriorating downtown complex with 130 affordable units for seniors. The city already approved a 1 million dollar demolition loan earlier this month after the Jacksonville Housing Authority abandoned an earlier renovate-in-place plan.

ANDREW: What's the actual hurdle today — is this just a formality?

JENNY: Not quite — the project needs the rezoning approved before demolition and construction can move forward, so today's vote is a real checkpoint, not a rubber stamp. We'll know more once the Commission votes this afternoon.

JENNY: Separately, the City Council continues digesting Mayor Donna Deegan's proposed budget for the fiscal year that starts in October — 2.03 billion dollars, according to the Jacksonville Daily Record, a 1.1 percent increase driven mostly by public safety raises, with no property tax rate hike and, for the second year running, no draw from reserves. Public safety alone accounts for over half the general fund. The mayor is holding a series of town halls for public input as the Council works through it.

JENNY: There's also movement on the JEA capacity fee story we've been following. Council President Nick Howland has stood up a new Financial Audit and Oversight committee, which took effect July 20th, replacing the old special investigatory panel and narrowing the focus specifically to the uncollected fees. JEA's own chief administrative officer testified under oath last month that the utility failed to collect an estimated 25 million dollars over 29 years. The new committee has until September 18th to report findings and recommendations to the Council.

JENNY: And on a lighter note, the Jaguars open training camp to the public July 29th at the Miller Electric Center, with free tickets for ten open practice dates running through late August, including the Teal and White scrimmage on August 7th.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: the Fed's meeting next Tuesday and Wednesday, July 28th and 29th. Going in, rate-hike odds are unusually unsettled because of the oil shock, and Chair Warsh will be making that call with an open ethics review hanging over one of his own governors. Watch whether the committee holds steady or whether nine officials now projecting a 2026 hike translates into an actual move — and watch oil prices between now and then, because another push toward 100 dollars a barrel could tilt the decision. We'll also be watching for Freddie Mac's own weekly rate print later today, our first real read on whether this oil spike is already bleeding into mortgage pricing.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.
